\section{Where things stand}

\begin{center}
{\small
\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{@{}L{3.3cm}L{2.6cm}Y@{}}
\rowcolor{TableHead}
\textbf{Block} & \textbf{State} & \textbf{One-line result} \\
\midrule
Week 1 --- data & Closed & Three public datasets, windowed, no windows dropped \\
Week 2 --- simple models & Closed & On WESAD, logistic regression reaches 0.92 \\
Week 3 --- a published number & Closed & We did not reproduce Health-LLM's 0.76 \\
Weeks 4--6 --- real recordings & Closed & Best language-model score is 0.60; plots are at chance \\
Your comparison request & Done & Prompting and fine-tuning kept in separate tables \\
Weeks 7--8 --- replacements & Closed & Noise collapses WESAD; spectrum and ``same condition'' do not \\
Week 9 --- adjectives & Not started & Strip the words, then flip them \\
Week 10 --- one summary ratio & Not started & Only after Week 9 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
}
\end{center}

The short version. On WESAD, logistic regression on ordinary heart and skin
features reaches 0.92. The best language model on the real recording reaches
0.60. Showing the model a plot instead of numbers does nothing: it sits at
chance. When I replace the recording, Gaussian noise, a flat line, an empty
prompt, and another person in the wrong condition all fall to that same chance
line. Two replacements do not. A phase-randomized ECG, which keeps the
spectrum, still scores 0.88 with logistic regression. Another person who was
in the same condition scores 0.95. The language model, when it is reading
feature sentences, follows that pattern and even exaggerates it.

\section{The study, in one paragraph}

A run of papers now claims that a language model can tell stress or mental workload
from a wearable. They rarely check whether the model needed the recording. I take
three public lab datasets, show each 60-second window to an open model in three
ways, and then replace the recording with noise, with another person, or with
nothing. If the score survives, the model was not reading that trace. The sharper
test, still to come, is whether it is reading the numbers or the adjectives around
them (``elevated heart rate, stress-typical''). Either outcome is worth reporting.
That was filed before these runs, at \url{https://osf.io/62r5t}.

The model does not write a paragraph. For each window I look at the probability
of two letters. \texttt{A} is the calmer class (non-stress, low workload, or
rest). \texttt{B} is the harder class (stress, high workload, or Stroop).
Whichever letter is more probable is the prediction. The wording of the prompt
was chosen on two people and then left alone. Those two people are not in the
scores below. For the verbalized features, the words ``high'' and ``low'' are
set from the other people, never from the person being scored. There is no
training of the language model on WESAD, MAUS, or CogWear. Fine-tuning appears
only in the Health-LLM comparison, because that paper fine-tuned.

\section{The three datasets}

Each example is one minute of a recording, and the next window starts 30 seconds
later, so neighbors overlap. A window never crosses from one condition into
another. WESAD is the standard lab stress set: a public speaking task against
calm and a comedy clip, from a chest belt and a wristband, 15 people. MAUS is
easy versus hard n-back, from a wrist pulse, 22 people. CogWear
is a color-word Stroop against rest, from a wristband, 10 people. None of the
windows were dropped for missing samples.

\begin{center}
{\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lcccc@{}}
\toprule
\rowcolor{TableHead}
\textbf{Dataset} & \textbf{People} & \textbf{Windows} & \textbf{Class split} & \textbf{Dropped} \\
\midrule
WESAD & 15 / 15 & 1{,}042 & 731 non-stress / 311 stress & 0 \\
MAUS & 22 / 22 & 1{,}086 & 362 low / 724 high & 0 \\
CogWear & 10 / 11 & 114 & 39 baseline / 75 Stroop & 0 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
}
\end{center}

CogWear subject~3 is out because PhysioNet is missing that person's EDA file. The
feature code is frozen (NeuroKit2 0.2.13). The same code feeds the linear model
and the feature sentences, so those two are looking at the same numbers.

\section{What a simple model can already do}

Before any language model ran, I fit a logistic regression and a small decision
tree on the same features the sentences are built from. The shuffle ceiling is
a sanity check: shuffle the labels inside each person, refit a thousand times,
and take the score that 95\% of those shuffles fall below. A real model has to
clear that line. ``Guessing'' is always picking the more common class.

\begin{center}
{\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lccccc@{}}
\toprule
\rowcolor{TableHead}
\textbf{Dataset} & \textbf{Logistic reg.} & \textbf{Small tree} & \textbf{Guessing} & \textbf{Shuffle ceiling} & \textbf{Signal} \\
\midrule
WESAD ($n{=}15$) & 0.918 & 0.848 & 0.412 & 0.433 & Strong \\
MAUS ($n{=}22$) & 0.444 & 0.482 & 0.400 & 0.413 & Weak \\
CogWear ($n{=}10$) & 0.569 & 0.560 & 0.397 & 0.541 & Weak \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
}
\end{center}

WESAD is the dataset that can test whether a model is using the recording. A linear
model is far above chance there, so an LLM that ignores the trace has a high score
to miss. MAUS and CogWear are weak even for logistic regression. On those two, a
language-model score near 0.4 is not evidence of anything, and the ratio we
pre-registered for later will often be undefined. The raw gap is what I will report.

\begin{figure}[!ht]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth,height=2.15in,keepaspectratio]{figures/fig_floors_vs_llm.pdf}
\caption{Best simple model against the best language-model score on the real
recording. Each language-model bar is the best of that model's three settings.
WESAD is the only dataset where the simple model is far above guessing.}
\end{figure}

\section{Checking one published number before trusting the pipeline}

The plan was filed publicly before the language-model grid ran
(\url{https://osf.io/62r5t}). Three predictions are on that filing, and none of
them are scored yet. I expect plots and raw number-lists to lose most of their
advantage once the recording is replaced. I expect the worded features to lose
more than half their advantage once the adjectives are stripped. I expect
flipped adjectives (``low'' where the value is high) to change the prediction
on more than 40\% of windows. Week 10 is where those get a single number.
Week 9 is the adjective half.

As a check that I was running the published method and not a lookalike, I
reproduced one Health-LLM setting before the rest of the grid: PMData stress,
MedAlpaca-7B, no examples in the prompt. Their paper says MAE $0.76 \pm 0.1$.
This rerun is $\mathbf{2.689 \pm 0.038}$. The answers are often ``out of 5'' or
``out of 10'', and the scorer, which was fixed in advance, reads the first
number, so it records 5 or 10. I left that rule alone. The gap is part of the
result, not a bug I papered over.

\begin{figure}[!ht]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.58\textwidth]{figures/fig_anchor_mae.pdf}
\caption{The published Health-LLM number ($0.76\pm 0.1$) next to this rerun
($2.689\pm 0.038$). Lower is better. The gap is the result.}
\end{figure}

The models in the rest of this report are open weights: Qwen3-8B and
Llama-3.1-8B for text, and Qwen2.5-VL-7B for plots. The registration originally
named a GPT model. That path was dropped because the account was capped at 50
requests a day, and the registration has a public note saying so.

prompt. ``128 averages'' chops the minute into 128 bins and averages inside
each bin. ``Sentences'' are the feature lines. The two
people used to pick the wording are WESAD S2 and S8, MAUS 015 and 023, and
CogWear 4 and 8. No window failed to score.

The bold row is the best language-model result in the study so far: Qwen, on

\section{Showing the model a plot instead}

Qwen2.5-VL-7B sees a line drawing of the chest ECG on WESAD, or the wrist pulse
on MAUS. The drawing has no name and no class on it. The same window always
makes the same file. CogWear has no plot condition. The prompt here includes
four example plots, chosen before these scores.

\begin{center}
{\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lccc@{}}
\toprule
\rowcolor{TableHead}
\textbf{Dataset} & \textbf{Prompt} & \textbf{macro-F1 [95\% CI]} & \textbf{Windows} \\
\midrule
WESAD & four example plots & 0.412 [0.410, 0.414] & 906 \\
MAUS & four example plots & 0.400 [0.399, 0.400] & 990 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
}
\end{center}

Both sit on chance, and the intervals are tight because the model almost always
picks the same class. That is what we expected for plots. I have not gone back
and rewritten the plot prompt to chase a higher number.

\begin{figure}[!ht]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth,height=2.15in,keepaspectratio]{figures/fig_paradigm_c.pdf}
\caption{The plot condition next to guessing and next to Qwen's number and word

\section{What you asked for: a matched comparison}

After the last meeting you asked for recent papers, from a real venue, and for
the comparison to stay matched. Same public dataset, same open model, and
prompting next to prompting, fine-tuning next to fine-tuning. A WESAD macro-F1
does not belong next to a paper that reports MAE on daily step counts.

The paper that meets that bar is Health-LLM (Kim et al., CHIL 2024). The task
is PMData stress, a score from 1 to 5. The metric is mean absolute error: how
far the predicted score is from the person's own rating. Lower is better. The inputs are
two weeks of steps, calories, resting heart rate, sleep, and that day's mood.
The model with public weights is MedAlpaca-7B. Their Table~3 is frozen
prompting. Their Table~4 is the same model after fine-tuning. SensorLM
(NeurIPS 2025) is a conference paper in the same area, but the weights and the
Fitbit corpus are not public, so it is not in these tables.

The zero-shot rerun uses their prompt and the locked 299-item eval. The
first-number scorer was fixed before the run. Many completions say ``out of 5''
or ``out of 10'', and the scorer reads 5 or 10. That is why our MedAlpaca MAE
is far above theirs. I did not change the scorer to close the gap.

\begin{center}
{\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}llcc@{}}
\toprule
\rowcolor{TableHead}
\textbf{Row} & \textbf{Model} & \textbf{Adaptation} & \textbf{MAE} \\
\midrule
Paper Table 3 & MedAlpaca-7b & no examples & $0.76 \pm 0.1$ \\
This rerun & MedAlpaca-7b & no examples & $2.689 \pm 0.038$ \\
Our model, their prompt & Qwen3-8B & no examples & $0.795 \pm 0.020$ \\
Our model, their prompt & Llama-3.1-8B & no examples & $2654 \pm 43$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{center}

\noindent Qwen answers \texttt{Answer: 3}. Llama writes Python that pastes step counts;
the locked first-number scorer reads those counts. The scorer was not changed.
Always answering 3 on this eval has MAE 0.401, which is still below Qwen.

\begin{center}
{\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}llcc@{}}
\toprule
\rowcolor{TableHead}
\textbf{Row} & \textbf{Model} & \textbf{Adaptation} & \textbf{MAE} \\
\midrule
Paper Table 4 & MedAlpaca-7b & fine-tuned on PMData & 0.38 \\
This rerun & MedAlpaca-7b & fine-tuned, small adapter & 2.697 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{center}

297 of 299 fine-tuned answers parsed. They still say ``out of 5'', so the
scorer still reads 5. The same model's zero-shot seed on this eval was 2.714.
Fine-tuning did not move it. Their published fine-tuned error is 0.38. Ours is
2.70. Training follows their 7B recipe: 3 epochs, batch 128, learning rate
$2\times 10^{-5}$, and the small adapter from the MedAlpaca defaults. I did not
oversample, because they never published the rule, and I skipped the 100-step
warmup, because this training set is only 653 rows. Qwen, on their prompt,
lands near their paper number and still loses to always answering 3 (error
0.401 on this split). Llama does not answer with a stress score. It writes
Python, and the scorer reads a step count out of that code.

\section{Weeks 7--8 --- what survives when the recording is replaced}

The prompts stay frozen. For each window I swap the trace and score again.
There are five replacements that are meant to destroy the signal, and one that
is not. That last one keeps the condition and changes the person. It answers a
different question: is the model using this recording, or the fact that
stressed people look alike? It is in the tables. It is not a null.

\begin{figure}[!ht]
\centering
\begin{tikzpicture}[
  rung/.style={
    draw=Accent, fill=TableHead, rounded corners=1.5pt, align=center,
    font=\footnotesize, inner sep=3pt, minimum height=0.72cm, text width=2.15cm
  },
  keep/.style={rung, fill=white, draw=Ask}
]
\node[rung] (g) {Gaussian\\noise};
\node[rung, right=0.18cm of g] (i) {phase\\randomized};
\node[rung, right=0.18cm of i] (b) {wrong person,\\wrong condition};
\node[rung, right=0.18cm of b] (f) {flat line};
\node[rung, right=0.18cm of f] (d) {nothing\\left};
\node[keep, below=0.55cm of b] (p) {wrong person,\\same condition\\[-1pt]\scriptsize not a null};
\end{tikzpicture}
\caption{The five replacements that are meant to wipe the class, and the one
underneath that keeps it on purpose.}
\end{figure}

One hundred and twenty settings were scored this way, with no failed windows.
The probability of each letter is saved with every window. Before looking at
the language models, the same features go through the same logistic regression
as in Week~2. That table says how much class information each replacement still
holds. A replacement is not assumed to be empty. It is measured.

Classical logistic regression on those features:

\begin{center}
{\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lccc@{}}
\toprule
\rowcolor{TableHead}
\textbf{Replacement} & \textbf{WESAD} & \textbf{MAUS} & \textbf{CogWear} \\
\midrule
Gaussian noise & 0.412 & 0.400 & 0.486 \\
Phase-randomized & 0.880 & 0.405 & 0.458 \\
Wrong person, wrong condition & 0.411 & 0.405 & 0.380 \\
Flat line & 0.412 & --- & 0.397 \\
Signal deleted & --- & --- & --- \\
Same condition, other person & 0.954 & 0.494 & 0.773 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{center}

A dash means there was nothing to fit. A flat MAUS pulse has no heartbeats, so
the features are empty. Deleting the signal leaves no features on any dataset.

Read the WESAD column from the top. Noise, a flat line, and a window from the
wrong person in the wrong condition all fall to 0.41, which is the majority
floor. A phase-randomized ECG, which keeps the spectrum and throws away the
waveform, is still at 0.88. Another stressed person's recording, with the
label kept, is at 0.95. So on this dataset the class is mostly in the spectrum
and in the kind of person, not in one individual's pulse shape. MAUS and
CogWear never had that strong a classical signal, and the ladder does not
create one.

\begin{figure}[!ht]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig_ledger.pdf}
\caption{Logistic regression on each replacement. The missing MAUS flat-line
bar is the empty-feature case above, not a score of zero. The dashed line is
guessing on WESAD.}
\end{figure}

The same replacements were then given to the frozen prompts. Below is Qwen3-8B
on WESAD, the only place a language model had cleared chance on the real
recording. Llama's intervals all touch guessing or sit under it, so a second
chart would not show a pattern. Green is the real recording.
Brown keeps the condition and changes the person. Teal is a null. The legend
is on the figure.

\begin{figure}[!ht]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig_surrogate_qwen.pdf}
\caption{Qwen3-8B on WESAD, held-out people only. Left: ECG as 128 averages
(0.60 on the real recording). Right: feature sentences (0.58 on the real
recording). Green is the real recording. Teal bars are the null replacements.
Brown keeps the stress label and changes the person. A flat line and an empty
prompt sit on chance. Sentences built from a phase-randomized trace score 0.70,
higher than the real recording. Sentences from another stressed person score 0.83.}
\end{figure}

That last pair is the result I want on the table. When the words in the prompt
are built from features that still contain the class, Qwen does well even if
the waveform is no longer the original person's. When the features are noise
or absent, Qwen falls to chance or below it. The raw-ECG setting moves less. It
was only modestly above chance to begin with, and several replacements stay in
that same band. The dependence score that turns these gaps into one ratio is
Week 10. It is not in this PDF.

\section{What is left}

Week 9 is the adjective test, on the feature sentences only. Three wordings of
the same numbers: as they are now, with the evaluative words removed, and with
those words flipped. There is an optional fourth wording, SensorLM's plain
statistical sentences (mean, max, min, spread), with none of their activity or
mood lines. I would like a yes or no on that fourth wording before I freeze
the set.

Week 10 turns the gaps in this report into one ratio per condition,
\[
\mathrm{SDS}
=
\frac{M_{\mathrm{real}}-M_{\mathrm{surrogate}}}{M_{\mathrm{real}}-M_{\mathrm{chance}}},
\]
where $M$ is macro-F1 and $M_{\mathrm{chance}}$ is the shuffle floor from Week~2.
If the real recording was never convincingly above that floor, the ratio is
left blank and only the gap is shown. MAUS and CogWear are where that will
happen. The ratio is not in this PDF.
